Historically, Android has only supported 4 KB memory page sizes, which has optimized system memory performance for the average amount of total memory that Android devices have typically had. Beginning with Android 15, AOSP supports devices that are configured to use a page size of 16 KB (16 KB devices). If your app uses any NDK libraries, either directly or indirectly through an SDK, then you will need to rebuild your app for it to work on these 16 KB devices.

The Android Studio build system is based on Gradle, and the Android Gradle plugin adds several features that are specific to building Android apps. Although the Android plugin is typically updated in lock-step with Android Studio, the plugin (and the rest of the Gradle system) can run independent of Android Studio and be updated separately.

"Android 15 introduced support for 16 KB memory pages to optimize performance of the platform. Android 16 adds a compatibility mode, allowing some apps built for 4 KB memory pages to run on a device configured for 16 KB memory pages.
If Android detects that your app has 4 KB aligned memory pages, it automatically uses compatibility mode and display a notification dialog to the user. Setting the android:pageSizeCompat property in the AndroidManifest.xml to enable the backwards compatibility mode will prevent the display of the dialog when your app launches. For best performance, reliability, and stability, your app should still be 16 KB aligned."

Jetpack Compose is Android’s modern toolkit for building native UI. It simplifies and accelerates UI development on Android. Quickly bring your app to life with less code, powerful tools, and intuitive Kotlin APIs.

Compose Multiplatform is a modern declarative and reactive UI framework developed by JetBrains that provides a simple way to build user interfaces with a small amount of Kotlin code. It also allows you to write your UI once and run it on any of the supported platforms – iOS, Android, desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux), and web.

"Kotlin is an open source statically typed programming language that targets the JVM, Android, JavaScript, Wasm, and Native. It's developed by JetBrains. Kotlin is a modern but already mature programming language designed to make developers happier. It's concise, safe, interoperable with Java and other languages, and provides many ways to reuse code between multiple platforms for productive programming."

"Each row is one CPU core and the horizontal axis is time.
Color shows IPC: red is low, yellow is medium, and green is high. Darkness shows cycles intensity, so darker cells mean that core was busier at that time. Gray cells mean there was no valid cycles or instructions sample.
Focus on dark cells: dark green means the CPU was busy and completed more instructions per cycle. Dark red or yellow means it spent many cycles but completed fewer instructions, possibly waiting on cache or memory, or running through an inefficient pipeline. Light cells usually mean that core was not doing much work."
IPC/Cycles Heatmap is available with Metric Pro.

"IPC = total instructions / total cycles. The green line is the overall IPC after summing all cores.
Cycles only show how much CPU clock time was spent. Instructions are closer to the actual work completed. IPC tells whether that clock time was used efficiently.
Do not judge efficiency by cycles alone. High cycles with high IPC usually means the CPU was busy and productive. High cycles with low IPC usually means the CPU was busy, but execution efficiency was low."
CPU IPC analysis is available with Metric Pro.

"CPU Usage Normalized weights traditional CPU usage by the current CPU frequency. Total = CPU Usage × (sum of current CPU frequencies / sum of maximum CPU frequencies).
Why use it: mobile CPU frequency changes constantly. With traditional CPU utilization, 30% at a low frequency and 30% at a high frequency produce the same value, even though the high-frequency case consumes substantially more performance. Traditional CPU utilization therefore cannot accurately reflect performance consumption. A normalized, quantifiable statistic is needed to include frequency in the measurement."

"Small Jank is usually not very noticeable. Jank and Big Jank are intended to reflect stutter that is perceptible in real use.
The Jank detection algorithm is designed to reflect perceptible stutter. It does not directly record every low-FPS interval, gradual FPS decline, or partial FPS drop as a stutter event.
As a result, the Jank count may be lower than that reported by tools that make determinations directly from Frame Time values."

"This device is using GED to read GPU frequency.
Root mode usually reports GED's virtual OPP frequency. It is a virtual performance level defined by the GPU scheduler's full GPU capability range. It indicates the current performance level and may not equal the hardware clock at this moment.
The non-root GED path reports the effective frequency after DCS (Dynamic Core Scaling). DCS adjusts the value according to the number of GPU cores currently enabled and their workload, so low values such as 8, 13, or 26 MHz may appear.
This is a normal difference in measurement semantics. It does not mean that reading failed or that GPU performance is abnormal."
